title: Realism VS Accuracy: Event Sequence Forecasting from a Generative Modeling Perspective
claim: The prediction that scores best on accuracy metrics matches no realistic outcome, so accuracy and distributional realism conflict.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right timeline, amount vs time, legend with check/cross marks
description: A single toy example drawn as an amount-versus-time plot. A bold 'Bet on black' node sits at the bottom left, after a grey 'Coffee $4' node. Two realistic chains branch from it. The blue 'Won' chain climbs steeply through Taxi $35, Restaurant $90 and Karaoke $70. The green 'Lost' chain stays low through Bus $2, Hot dog $3 and Movie rental $4. A red dashed 'Prediction' chain runs between them: Bus $18, Hot dog $46, Movie rental $36. Each event is a rounded pill with an icon and a dollar amount. A legend at top left lists Won (49%), Lost (51%) and Prediction. Each has green check or red cross marks for realism and accuracy. The prediction gets a cross on realism and a check on accuracy, and the two real chains get the opposite.
caption: A toy event sequence. After a bet on black at roulette, the evening follows one of two realistic chains of transactions: the person either lost (51%) or won (49%). The prediction that minimizes MSE and maximizes per-event accuracy takes the categories of the more likely chain and averages the amounts, pairing cheap categories with large sums (e.g., an \$18 bus ride). It scores best on predictive metrics, yet matches neither chain. On the other hand, each possible outcome is realistic, but its expected MSE is about twice as large.
abstract: Event sequences are chains of random events, each described by heterogeneous (numerical and categorical) features. The problem of event sequence forecasting occurs in finance, healthcare, business process intelligence, and other fields. In this work, we study multi-horizon forecasting of event sequences as a conditional generative modeling problem. We evaluate forecasts not only for prediction accuracy, but also for distributional realism. To this end, we present a benchmark comprising metrics for both quality aspects, strong statistical baselines, recent models adapted from adjacent fields, and curated real-world datasets. Careful evaluation reveals that no method excels at both accuracy and realism, highlighting a fundamental trade-off between the two. Finally, we introduce Wasserstein BaryBooster, an algorithm that aggregates samples from a realism-strong diffusion model into a state-of-the-art predictor, demonstrating that distributional realism can be converted into prediction accuracy. Code is available at https://github.com/xaosina/event-sequence-forecasting.
